title: The whirlwind
hook: a whirlwind doesn't last all morning; speak little (Tao Te Ching 23)

segments.voice: Yesterday, chapter twenty-two, and your line was yield and be whole. Did you give way on one small point? Did anything move that had been stuck? Day one thousand eighty-five.

The sky goes green-gray in the middle of the afternoon. Wind tears through the street, a trash can rolls past on its side, rain comes down so hard it bounces. Everyone ducks into doorways. And then, almost before the shirts are soaked, it's over. The gutters are still running, but the sun is out, and someone is already wiping off a café chair. While a storm like that is happening, it can seem as if it will never stop. They don't. Chapter twenty-three of the Tao Te Ching watches one blow through, and draws a lesson about how much we say.
screen: `THE SKY GOES GREEN-GRAY.` → `EVERYONE DUCKS.` → `THEN IT'S OVER.`

segments.voice: First, speak little, like nature. The chapter opens with just a few characters that link saying little with what is so of itself, the natural way of things. Nature doesn't talk much. It doesn't explain itself. Second, no storm lasts all morning. Then the example, in Legge's translation: "A violent wind does not last for a whole morning; a sudden rain does not last for the whole day." Who makes the wind and the rain? Heaven and earth, the chapter says. And if even heaven and earth can't keep up a burst like that for long, how much less can a person. A rant, a lecture, a flood of messages late at night: loud and fast runs out. Third, you become what you follow. The chapter then says that whoever follows the Way becomes one with the Way. Whoever follows virtue becomes one with virtue. And whoever follows loss becomes one with loss. What you keep company with, you turn into, and the Way, it adds, is glad to have you. Fourth, trust that isn't enough. The chapter closes with a line the book used before, in chapter seventeen: where trust falls short, there is no trust in return. Too many words can be a sign of that. People who trust each other don't need to keep talking. This also closes a week. It began with leaders whose people said we did it ourselves, then the way lost and the rules that came after, the uncarved block, drifting like an infant, the elusive and real, yielding to be whole, and now the whirlwind that doesn't last.
screen: `SPEAK LITTLE, LIKE NATURE.` · `NO STORM LASTS ALL MORNING.` · `YOU BECOME WHAT YOU FOLLOW.` · `TRUST THAT ISN'T ENOUGH.` · then, large: `A VIOLENT WIND DOES NOT LAST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say it in fewer words. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you need to say to someone today: a request, an answer, an apology, a no. Say it silently the long way first, with every reason and every softener. Then say it again in half the words. Then once more, keeping only what's needed. Notice how short it becomes. Then sit in the quiet after that last, plain version, and let it be enough. The bell holds the time.
The whirlwind. Chapter twenty-three's violent wind that can't last a whole morning, and its advice to say little, the way nature does. Today's word.
Your line: speak little. Say less today: one fewer explanation, one shorter message, one moment where you let silence answer. Day one thousand eighty-five, and a week done.

howItsDone: Some people who read the Tao Te Ching take chapter twenty-three as a practice of restraint in speech: saying what is needed, then stopping, and letting strong feelings pass before they talk.

fork.setup: you're in the middle of a whirlwind of a conversation, loud and fast. what does chapter twenty-three suggest?
options: say little, and let the storm blow itself out.
keep sending messages so nothing is left unsaid.
fork.reveal: a violent wind doesn't last a whole morning. the chapter opens with saying little, the natural way of things.

original.note: Chinese, xī yán zìrán: few words, what is so of itself. The opening of Tao Te Ching 23.

trapdoor: what you thought: the whirlwind is a story about a storm.
what it means: even heaven and earth can't keep a storm going, so a flood of words won't last either; say little.
what a scholar hears: xi yan ziran, few words and the natural, the chapter's opening, and a closing line on trust repeated from chapter seventeen.

notes: Verify the Legge 1891 wording: 'A violent wind does not last for a whole morning; a sudden rain does not last for the whole day.'
The rest of chapter 23 is paraphrased, including 'the Way is glad to have you' (the Way, virtue and loss each 'gladly receive' the one who follows them, in many readings). Confirm.
The closing line on trust (信不足焉，有不信焉) also appears in chapter 17 in the received text; some editions place it differently. Confirm before keeping the myth item about it.
Week end (days 1079–1085) is recapped by title in the teach; days 1079–1081 were not on disk when this was drafted, so the recap follows their index lines.
The storm scene is an illustration, not a source. 'Loud and fast runs out' is a gloss on the chapter, not a quotation; soften if needed.
Pronunciation guide for 希言自然 is approximate.
